title: AI-assisted development without surrendering verification
summary: Use Genie Code (formerly Databricks Assistant) to explain code, draft a transformation, investigate an error and construct tests, keep every request inside the permission and confidentiality boundary, and judge every suggestion against an expected result you computed yourself.
objectives: Name the assistant as the documentation names it, list the context it sends to the model and the permission boundary that bounds it, and state what must never be pasted.
Write bounded requests to explain, draft, diagnose and test, each with the tables, grain, counting rules and expected count that make the answer checkable.
Catch a suggested many-to-many join that inflates totals by computing expected rows by hand, correct it at the right grain with a documented source, and reject a fix that hides an error.
Keep an assistance record so a reviewer can see the request, the evidence and the verdict.

questions.prompt: Order 1001 has two order lines (250 and 150) and two shipments (10 and 5). The authored draft inner-joins order lines to shipments on order_id and sums amount and shipped_qty. How many joined rows does 1001 produce, and what does it contribute?

options.text: Four rows, contributing 800 to revenue and 30 to shipped quantity.
options.rationale: Every line pairs with every shipment of the same order, 2 × 2 = 4, so each amount and each quantity is read twice: (250 + 150) × 2 and (10 + 5) × 2.

options.text: Two rows, contributing 400 and 15, because each line meets its own shipment.
options.rationale: No column pairs a line with a particular shipment; the join key is order_id alone, so each line matches both shipments.

options.text: Four rows, contributing 800 to revenue but a correct 15 to quantity, because quantity lives at shipment grain.
options.rationale: Quantity is right only when the order has one line; here each shipment also pairs with two lines, so its quantity is read twice.

options.text: Two rows, contributing 800 and 15, because only the amounts are repeated.
options.rationale: The row count and the sums are inconsistent: two rows cannot carry each amount twice, and a many-to-many key repeats both measures.

questions.prompt: An engineer asks the assistant to draft a query over a table they have no SELECT privilege on. According to the documented boundary, what does the assistant send to the model about that table?

options.text: Nothing beyond what the engineer's own Unity Catalog permissions allow; the context respects those permissions.
options.rationale: Documented: all context sent to the model respects the user's Unity Catalog permissions, so the assistant cannot see more than the engineer can.

options.text: The table's data samples, because metadata and samples are read with a service identity.
options.rationale: The documentation states the opposite: the assistant is bounded by the user's permissions and can only access what they can.

options.text: The full table, because the model needs it to draft correct SQL.
options.rationale: No feature is documented as sending whole tables, and permission-bounded context would exclude this table entirely.

options.text: Only the table name, since names are public across the workspace.
options.rationale: Names are not public across a workspace; catalog privileges govern visibility, and the answer is bounded by the engineer's grants, not a name-only rule.

questions.prompt: A quarter filter on shipped_at fails because one row reads 2026/09/05 instead of 2026-09-05. A suggested quick fix replaces CAST with try_cast and the error disappears. What happened to that row?

options.text: It now parses to NULL, so the filter silently drops it and its 20 units leave the total.
options.rationale: try_cast returns NULL instead of raising on malformed input; the row is not fixed, it is discarded without a message.

options.text: It parses correctly, because try_cast accepts more date formats than CAST.
options.rationale: try_cast performs the same conversions as CAST; it changes only what happens when the conversion fails.

options.text: It raises a warning in the cell output but stays in the result.
options.rationale: No warning is produced; the documented behaviour is a NULL result, which is exactly what makes the fix dangerous.

options.text: It is kept with its original text and excluded only if the filter compares strings.
options.rationale: The cast produces NULL for that row, and a comparison with NULL is never true, so the filter cannot keep it.

cards.prompt: Which names does the documentation use for the workspace coding assistant, and which similar name is a different feature?
cards.answer: Genie Code on current pages and Databricks Assistant on former-name pages, for one coding assistant; Genie Agents is a separate natural-language feature for business users.
cards.explanation: The landing page is titled Genie Code and describes generating and running code, building pipelines and dashboards, debugging errors and working with Unity Catalog data. Former-name pages such as What is Databricks Assistant? still describe the same assistant, and some former addresses are now indexed under Genie Code titles. Genie Agents, formerly Genie spaces, answer business users' plain-English questions over curated tables; keep the names apart when you search.

cards.prompt: What context does the assistant send to the model with your prompt?
cards.answer: Table and column names, descriptions, the code you are working on, data samples from tables and cell outputs, plus anything attached or referenced with @.
cards.explanation: The usage page lists this context, and the tips page shows how to attach tables, notebooks, queries and files explicitly. Everything sent respects your Unity Catalog permissions, so the model's view is bounded by your own grants. Knowing the list matters both ways: it tells you what to attach for a better draft and what is already leaving the notebook when you press Enter.

cards.prompt: Name three things that must never go into an assistant request, even though the model partner retains nothing.
cards.answer: Credentials or tokens, personal data about identifiable people, and bulk customer or supplier records beyond a small labelled sample.
cards.explanation: Databricks states that partners do not retain submitted data and that submissions are not used to train generative foundation models it offers to third parties. That is a retention statement, not a licence: a pasted token sits in a transcript and a history, personal data may be governed by your policy, and a full export is more than the request needs. Replace secrets with placeholders, attach a small labelled sample, and list what was withheld in the record.

cards.prompt: What must a bounded request state before the assistant drafts a transformation?
cards.answer: The tables, the grain of the answer, the columns, the counting rules that could be misread, and the expected row count on a fixture.
cards.explanation: The tips page asks for specific prompts and a stated response structure; grain and expected count are added because they are what a wrong draft usually gets wrong. 'Revenue by customer' invites a join that multiplies; 'one row per customer, amount once per line, quantity once per shipment, keep unshipped orders, two rows expected' does not. The count is the first thing you compare after the draft runs.

cards.prompt: How do you test an assistant's explanation of a query instead of believing it?
cards.answer: Trace one concrete record through the code and check whether each claim in the explanation holds for that record.
cards.explanation: An explanation is prose about code, and prose can be wrong while sounding complete. The authored example says the draft 'joins each order line to its shipment'; tracing order 1001 shows two lines meeting two shipments and therefore four joined rows, which the sentence hides. One record, followed clause by clause with its row counts written down, either confirms the explanation or finds the sentence that fails.

cards.prompt: Why did the suggested join inflate both revenue and quantity for Amberline Motors?
cards.answer: Order 1001 has two lines and two shipments, so the many-to-many join paired each line with each shipment and read every amount and quantity twice.
cards.explanation: An inner join returns every matching pair. Each measure therefore repeats once per match on the other side: 1001's amounts and quantities double, 1003's single 900 triples across three shipments while its quantities stay right. Amberline reads 1050 / 38 against 650 / 23. Per-key counts on both tables expose it: 1001 appears in both lists, which is the many-to-many signature.

cards.prompt: Where should the expected rows for a generated query come from?
cards.answer: From the fixture by hand or by a separate method, computed before the draft runs, never from the draft's own output.
cards.explanation: If the expected values are read off the draft, the test can only confirm that the draft agrees with itself. Computing 650 and 1020 from the five order-line rows, and 23 and 50 from the six shipment rows, takes a minute and gives a result the draft can fail against. Add the row count and the grand totals so a partial failure, such as a missing customer, cannot hide inside a matching per-row figure.

cards.prompt: How do you correct a many-to-many join without losing the unshipped order?
cards.answer: Reduce both detail tables to one row per order first, then LEFT JOIN the two results and sum per customer.
cards.explanation: Pre-aggregating only shipments fixes revenue but still reads 1001's 15 shipped units once per line, so Amberline's quantity stays 38; both sides must reach order grain. The LEFT JOIN keeps order 1004, which has no shipment, and COALESCE turns its missing quantity into 0. The documented LEFT JOIN returns all rows of the left reference with NULL where there is no match. DISTINCT is the tempting shortcut and collapses equal amounts such as the two 250 lines.

cards.prompt: A quick fix makes an error disappear. What decides whether you accept it?
cards.answer: Whether it resolves the cause or only silences the symptom, checked by reading the fixture row that raised the error.
cards.explanation: The documented quick fix proposes corrections you can accept and run, and error diagnosis handles harder cases; neither judges the result. Replacing CAST with try_cast removes a parse error by turning the bad row into NULL, which drops it from any filter. The row that raised the error is the test: after the fix, does it carry the right value, or has it vanished? A fix that changes the answer needs the same expected-result check as a draft.

cards.prompt: What may the assistant write in a test, and what must you write yourself?
cards.answer: It may draft the fixture loader and assertion scaffolding; the expected values and the list of checks are yours, computed independently.
cards.explanation: A generated test that asserts the current output is a snapshot of whatever the draft did, wrong included. Ask for the structure, then fill in expected rows, counts and sums from your own working, and add checks the draft cannot have anticipated: four rows after the join, one per order; no NULL parsed dates; two rows returned. The test plan in the assistance record names each expected value's source.

cards.prompt: What are the steps of the review gate before an assistant suggestion is accepted?
cards.answer: Read the diff, run it on a fixture, compare with the expected result, record request, verdict and evidence, then accept or reject.
cards.explanation: Accept and run is one click; the gate makes it a decision you can defend. Reading the diff catches a changed filter or a dropped column; the fixture run makes the comparison concrete; the record keeps the request and the verdict beside the code so a later reviewer can see what the assistant was asked and what proved the answer. The same gate applies to a fix and to a test.

cards.prompt: What does an assistance record contain, and why keep one?
cards.answer: The bounded request, the context attached and withheld, a summary of the suggestion, the expected result and its source, the observed result, the verdict and the correction.
cards.explanation: The record turns assisted work into reviewable work. Without it the code shows only the final query; with it a reviewer sees that revenue was expected to be 1670 before any query ran, that the draft returned 3750, why, and which documentation the correction rests on. It also holds the confidentiality list, so what left the notebook is known.
